rounds.headline: Two blockers and a keyboard trap. The planning drawer was white on white with no seam, so it sliced the Waiting column mid-word and erased Done entirely. The card's state rules were declared after its interaction rules at equal specificity, so Done and Next cards had no focus ring at all. And the completion circle, the one thing the board exists to do, was a bare span with no keyboard path.

worst.problem: The completion circle is not a control. It is a span: not focusable, no role, no aria state, no keyboard path, no active state. Its only feedback fires on hover of the whole card, so the circle looks armed while the cursor is 300px away.
worst.done: It is now a button with checkbox semantics, named by the task, with a 32px hit area that does not grow the 18px circle, and its own hover, active and focus. The card hints; the control answers one step darker.

worst.problem: `.card[data-done]` and `.card[data-next]` redeclare box-shadow after `:hover` and `:focus-visible` at equal specificity, so later wins. On the resting board the five Done cards and the milestone card have no hover edge, and because `outline: none` survives, no visible focus ring either.
worst.done: Every ring on a card now runs through one `--card-ring` custom property. States set only the token; hover, focus, selection and drag are declared last.

worst.problem: The planning drawer is white, on the same inset, with the same radius, with no ring, no shadow and no scrim, sitting on a white sheet that does not move. Waiting is cut mid-word, Done and its five cards vanish with no cue they exist.
worst.done: The sheet moves over and the ink floor shows through an 18px gutter, which draws the seam with the product's own elevation rule. The board switches to a scrolling track so no column is sliced, and the dock re-centres on the board it serves.

worst.problem: The dense header reads '5 of 32 done' while the Done tray immediately below it is labelled 9 and renders nine ticked cards. The board contradicts itself by four tasks in the one state that exists to prove it survives peak season.
worst.done: Every header fact is derived from the rendered task set. The total, the done count, the overdue count and the unscheduled count now all come from one accessor, and the empty state falls out of the same expression.

worst.problem: `.cardDots` sits at `opacity: 0` with pointer events live. On desktop a keyboard user tabs into a card and the focus ring paints on an invisible button. On touch, where hover never fires, the coarse rule inflates that invisible button to a 44x44 target.
worst.done: A control at zero opacity is now inert. The menu reveals on hover, focus-within and its own focus, and on a coarse pointer it is simply present and quieter.

worst.problem: One board scan carried four grammars for one fact: an elapsed duration, a deictic, a weekday and a date. The same state had two names in one frame: the header said '1 overdue', the card said '2 days late'.
worst.done: One grammar. Every chip states the day the work is due, formatted from real dates in the fixture against the pinned review clock. Lateness is carried entirely by the fill, which is what the direction claimed all along.

rounds.headline: Five of the seven seats independently found the same defect: the card's actions button was an opaque white square painting over content. On touch it severed every title mid-word; on hover it whited out most of the date chip, including the filled overdue chip the whole palette argument rests on.

worst.problem: On coarse pointers the menu is a permanently visible 44x44 button with a white fill, over a title row that reserves no space for it. In the 390px frame all three visible titles are severed mid-word with no ellipsis.
worst.done: Reserving a gutter fixed it and cost the title a whole line, so the answer is structural instead. The top-right of a card belongs to the time fact; the menu moved to the end of the foot row where the card's other quiet facts already live. Nothing moves when it appears, and it can never paint on content.

worst.problem: Drag is the board's defining gesture and it exists only for a pointer. There is no keyboard route for moving a task between columns, and at rest no card says it is draggable at all.
worst.done: Cards gained a grab cursor, and the keyboard move is specified, drawn and announced: space picks a card up into a lift without the tilt, the arrows walk it between columns. It has its own specimen on the card sheet.

worst.problem: Opening Planning silently deletes a status column. Five trays at 238px need 1190px inside the 884px the drawer leaves, so Waiting is sliced mid-word and Done is gone entirely with no cue it exists.
worst.done: Five trays now fit the narrowed board, and whatever still runs past the edge snaps and dissolves rather than being guillotined. The same edge treatment turns on wherever the board overflows, which is every width below 1200.

worst.problem: The board's grid row sizes to the tallest column, so every tray stretches to it and the tray's own overflow rule can never fire. Columns cannot scroll independently: reaching the foot of To do drags Done out of view.
worst.done: Each column is its own scroller now, and the dock's clearance sits at the foot of every one of them rather than once at the foot of the tallest.

worst.problem: Every spine item and every view tab is an anchor with no href. An anchor without href carries no role, so the product's entire navigation was a row of focusable generics inside a nav containing no links, and no element carried aria-current.
worst.done: They are buttons with accessible names and aria-current, with a reset so the change costs no pixels. The phone rule also stopped hiding tiles by matching their tooltip text.

worst.problem: Three of five columns state the same fact twice, three lines apart. Done reads 'Finished work stays visible.' then 'Finished work stays here, so you can see it.'
worst.done: One source per column. The tray note says what the column is for; the empty line says only that there is nothing in it, and only To do leads with an instruction, so an empty board has exactly one first move.

rounds.headline: UX rose to 8.0 and the minimum rose again, but UI composition dropped, because a new dominant defect surfaced that four of seven seats found independently: the dock and its scrim were erasing each column's Add task row. A panel that only ever goes up is not looking hard enough.

worst.problem: The dock is the largest floating object in the composition and it was placed with no regard for what sits beneath it. It erased the Add task row in two to four of five columns in every desktop frame, and half-dissolved a live card at peak density. The scrim existed only to blur the damage.
worst.done: The dock's band is reserved in real layout and the scrim is deleted. Nothing can sit under the dock any more, so every column gets its foot back, its rule runs to the sheet's edge, and the columns gain height rather than lose it.

worst.problem: A browser line clamp cuts at the character, so cards read 'dinner 5.30p...' and 'before we hold th...'. It is the one defect visible in every populated frame and it is exactly what separates typeset copy from text poured into a container.
worst.done: The renderer trims to the last whole word by binary search, keeps the full string on the element for the tooltip and for assistive technology, and the title lost the percentage floor that was pushing date chips off the card's edge.

worst.problem: Nothing anywhere on the board stated today's date, so every time chip floated without an anchor. The loudest object in the product, the filled ink overdue chip, said only '14 Jul': an operator could not tell two days late from two months.
worst.done: The header states today, first, and the season counter names the season it counts through rather than floating as an unexplained ordinal.

worst.problem: The direction's central claim is that status is carried by ink density and fill. That channel is entirely presentational: the chip's accessible name was a bare date, so overdue, due today and milestone were indistinguishable to anyone not looking at the screen.
worst.done: A visually hidden prefix now carries the same fact in words, and the trays became named regions with real headings instead of nameless sections that contributed nothing to the accessibility tree.

worst.problem: Every card was a tab stop with two more focusable children, so crossing the dense board was roughly ninety-six tab presses.
worst.done: One roving tab stop per column. Tab crosses the whole board in five presses and the arrows walk the column.

worst.problem: The account chip read DO, the initials of the words 'Demo operator', which belong to nobody on the board. Both cards in the Waiting column opened with the word Waiting, under a tray already headed WAITING and described as held by a reply.
worst.done: The operator is Orla, so the chip reads OR. The Waiting titles say what is being waited on rather than restating their own container.

rounds.headline: Every seat moved up and the spread closed to 0.4, but the round diagnosed the ceiling rather than a defect. Four seats independently reached the same conclusion by different routes: the board advertises a keyboard model, draws the picked-up card and the drop target, and implements none of it. Interaction called it the finding with the widest blast radius; Measured evidence found the roving tab stop reached five of thirty-two cards; Taste said the work is 'an extremely well-made kanban that happens to contain wedding words'. No amount of typographic remediation was going to move a seat past that.

worst.problem: Every card advertised 'Task, movable' and Space plus four arrows, the specimen sheet illustrated the picked-up state, and none of it existed. The per-tray roving tabindex meant only five of thirty-two cards could be focused at all, and the drop-target and moving states had nothing that could ever trigger them.
worst.done: The interaction layer is built. One tab stop for the whole board, arrows that walk it, Space to pick up, arrows to place, Space to drop, Escape to put it back exactly where it came from, a polite live region on every step and a pill at the foot of the sheet that says what is in the hand — present only while the hand is full. Pointer drag runs the same model. The tick completes a task and plays the one flourish in the product. The dense board went from 101 focusable elements in the tab order to 2. Checked end to end by scripts/design/interaction-check.mjs.

worst.problem: The card foot truncated simultaneously: .who, .tag and .hi all shrank in proportion to their own width, so 'Mara & …  High pri…' sat under four of six cards on the default 1440 board — including on the specimen sheet that exists to prove the card is correct. Three seats found it independently.
worst.done: Whose wedding it is never shrinks. The row yields in a stated order — area of the house first, then priority — and the word 'priority' is cut to 'High', with the full phrase kept in the accessible name. Zero ellipses on the resting board at 1440.

worst.problem: The filled ink chip is deliberately the loudest object on the sheet, it already knows the answer, and it was a span with no behaviour. On the dense board it read '1 overdue' above thirty-two cards with no way to see which one.
worst.done: It is the filter it looked like: a real button with aria-pressed that reduces all five trays to the late work and says so. The header's own counts still describe the whole project, so filtering can never change what '5 of 13 done' means.

worst.problem: Opening Planning re-laid the board at minmax(170px, 1fr), giving the product's primary object a 105px title measure against the 254px the specimen sheet designs it at — 'Men / u…' broken mid-word. The global :focus-visible rule also set border-radius at (0,1,1), squaring off the completion circle and every pill in the chrome for keyboard users.
worst.done: The card has one floor in every state; the drawer-open board uses the same 258px minimum and what does not fit scrolls and snaps. The focus rule sets an outline and nothing else. Both edge fades are now measured from the elements after layout, so a fade means something is actually hidden.

worst.problem: Four of five empty-column lines opened on the word 'Nothing' — the templated repetition on the one screen a new operator meets first — and the Done column's note, 'Finished work stays visible.', described the interface rather than the work, alone among five notes that describe the work.
worst.done: Two lines rewritten to say something true about the column rather than restate its emptiness, and the Done note now describes the work: 'Work that is finished and settled.'

worst.problem: The bottom edge of the tray was the only undesigned edge on the sheet. An overflowing column was guillotined mid-word with nothing to say there was more, and on the empty board the Add row sat 860px below the sentence it belongs to.
worst.done: The tray foot is designed. A column with more in it than fits dissolves into the same mask idiom the sheet's right edge uses, measured rather than always-on; an empty tray's body stops at its content so the Add row sits under the line it belongs to.

rounds.headline: Three seats dropped, one by 1.1. This was the first round graded by driving the file rather than reading frames, and the interaction layer built in round 4 turned out to punish the operator for using it: every repaint annihilated every scroll position and the focus point, Space on a checkbox picked the card up instead of ticking it, nothing committed was reversible, and the filter emptied the board with no way back. A panel that only goes up is not looking hard enough — this is the round that proves it is. Brand rose to 8.1 and is the first seat within striking distance of the gate.

worst.problem: Every state change replaced the whole sheet, so every scroll position and the focus point were annihilated. Measured: one tick on a phone threw the board from Done back to To Do; the dense board lost every column's place on every interaction, including columns the operator had not touched; any pointer completion dropped focus to <body>, eight tab stops from where they were. It fired on tick, drag, drop, filter and every arrow press.
worst.done: Place is captured before the write and restored in the same frame, on every path rather than only the keyboard one — each column's scroll by lane, the board's horizontal scroll, and the exact control that held focus, including chrome controls. Mandatory scroll-snap is suspended for the one frame the restore takes, which is what had been dragging the phone back to the first column.

worst.problem: Space on the tick — a role=checkbox, whose contract key is Space — picked the card up instead of ticking it, and Enter on the '...' actions button completed the task and flew it to Done without opening any menu. A labelled control performing an unrelated, unannounced and unreversible action is the worst class of keyboard defect, and both sat on the single tab stop the whole design is built around.
worst.done: The card's own controls answer for themselves: the delegated handler stands down for Space and Enter inside the tick or the menu, and each button's native activation runs. Proven by four assertions in the behaviour gate.

worst.problem: Nothing the board committed was reversible, and the filter was a dead end. Clicking the overdue chip emptied five columns, repeated one identical sentence four times, left the header asserting '5 of 13 done' directly above columns counting zero, and clearing the last overdue task destroyed the only control that could undo it — leaving an empty board and no way back.
worst.done: The foot strip is the board's one reversibility surface, with three states in priority order: what is in your hand, what you just finished with an Undo bound to Cmd/Ctrl+Z, and what the filter is hiding with a way out. The chip states the filter, the header stops asserting totals it is not showing, Escape clears it, and it releases itself when nothing is overdue. The board says it once, in one column, rather than five times.

worst.problem: The board silently deleted content. The word-safe trim ran once, inside the first paint, before the webfont had swapped in, and never again — the resize listener only re-measured the edge fades. So a note read 'Ceremony 2pm orchard, drinks terrace, dinner', a complete-looking sentence that had quietly dropped '5.30pm. Share...', with no ellipsis and no visual tell. A venue operator cannot know they are reading a fragment.
worst.done: The trim restores from the full string first, so it is idempotent and a line can grow back when its column widens, and it re-runs on fonts.ready, on resize and on every repaint. Zero silent clips at six widths, asserted in the gate. The clamp also moved off the title onto its row: overflow:hidden made the title establish a formatting context, which is a block's instruction to avoid a float rather than flow around it, so a wide date chip was stealing width from all three lines instead of one.

worst.problem: The blackest, loudest object on the board was a bare date the operator had to decode by arithmetic, and the one indigo in the entire view was an undecodable diamond. Ink density said how loud; nothing said why.
worst.done: Every chip states its own condition in one grammar: '2 days overdue', 'Milestone 1 Aug', 'Today'. The diamond is gone. The dock's keycap now says what the operator's keyboard actually has on it, and the tray control says 'Add here' so it cannot be confused with the dock's 'Add task' ten pixels below.

worst.problem: The tray body grew to fill its column, leaving a 246px ruled void between the last card and the control that appends to it, and under a filter four Add rows landed on one line with the fifth stranded 548px below — five identical controls reading as a rendering fault rather than a filter. The foot band had 10px of clearance above the dock and 18px below, and the carry pill materialised in the exact 36px band the Add rows occupy.
worst.done: The body sizes to its content and only fills when it has more than fits. The band is 18 and 18. The pill sits clear of the Add rows, and they stand down while it is up rather than being covered.

rounds.headline: Every seat recovered from the round-5 dip, and the round found two defects that made the direction's own written claims unreachable on the real board: the completion flight was dead code, and every outward ring on a card was being clipped by its own column scroller. Both had survived five rounds of frame-reading because neither is visible in a screenshot. The behaviour gate grew from 43 assertions to 73.

worst.problem: The board's one celebratory moment did not happen. Sampled over 40 consecutive frames after a tick: transform none on every one, data-flying alive for two milliseconds. Setting the FLIP offset and clearing it inside the same style-change event starts no transition, so the single act this product exists for was a silent teleport a thousand pixels to the right — and the only thing on the board designed to be felt remained the filled ink overdue chip, which is bad news.
worst.done: The card flies as a fixed-position copy over the whole sheet, because the real node lives inside a column scroller that would clip both it and its shadow. It carries the one heavy shadow in the product, lands, and then plays the check-draw beat that was also written and never wired. The gate samples the ghost across the flight rather than trusting an attribute.

worst.problem: overflow-y: auto on the tray forces overflow-x: auto, and the card measured exactly the scroller's client width, so every outward ring and shadow was clipped on both flanks. The keyboard focus ring rendered as two disconnected indigo arcs with no sides; the picked-up card the same; --lift, described in the source as the one heavy shadow that exists, was unreachable on the real board. The specimen sheet was the only place either rendered correctly, because it opted out of the same overflow.
worst.done: A 6px gutter inside the tray's own 12px padding, pulled back by an equal negative margin. Card measure unchanged at 234, column rhythm unchanged, no horizontal scrollbar, rings whole — all four asserted in the gate. The specimen sheet is now rendered by the same rules it documents.

worst.problem: Five of thirteen cards clip their note, and the clipped half is the operationally load-bearing half — "…they need the call by Thursday", "…before service notes are locked". Clicking the card, the title or the note did nothing at all. The only route to the full string was a native hover tooltip: unreachable by keyboard and unreachable on the iPad that sits on a venue desk. The board could not deliver the instruction a card exists to carry.
worst.done: Clicking a card opens its note in place, which is also the obvious thing it looked like and previously did nothing, and Enter does the same — which removes a destructive default key, since Enter used to complete the task.

worst.problem: On the dense board the arrows walked focus off the bottom of the column and nothing scrolled: from the fifth card on the focused card was outside its own scroller, by up to 509px, while the live region announced "Position 9 of 10 in To do". At 768 the drag could not cross the board at all — three of five columns were unreachable, so the board's defining gesture could not finish a task's journey.
worst.done: A tray-scoped vertical correction after focus, deliberately not a general scrollIntoView, which nudges the horizontally snapped board on a phone and undoes the scroll restore. Holding a dragged card at the board's edge walks it across, with mandatory snap suspended for the length of the gesture.

worst.problem: The filtered board told the operator the same fact four times in three vocabularies with two exits, and parked a board-scoped sentence in a column-scoped slot so it read as a claim about To do. Separately, the two most consequential keys in the interaction were labelled with a minimal pair — "Space put it down" and "Esc put it back" — one of which commits the move and one of which throws it away, read at a glance mid-move.
worst.done: The board states the filter once, at the foot, with the header chip left as the control. "Space drop it here" and "Esc cancel the move", with the announcements matched and the cancel line finally naming the task.

worst.problem: The date chip was 56% of the title measure at 1440 and 68% at 1280, and it reserved that width on line one only — so every dated card set a starved first line while lines two and three ran full width. The milestone card, the one indigo card the whole board is composed to make you look at, set "Menu" over "tasting at The Orchard" at every width tested.
worst.done: The chip carries the value and the fill carries the condition. This narrows round 5's visible strings and is recorded as a reversal rather than slipped in: the sentence moves to the accessible name, the tooltip and the specimen sheet, which now teaches the mapping instead of assuming it. Zero starved first lines at six widths.

rounds.headline: The best round, and the first where the seats were asked for an honest distance and gave one. Interaction reached 8.0 and states plainly that 9.5 is achievable inside the locked direction with nothing structural missing; Brand agrees and asks for a copy contract; Typography puts its own ceiling at 8.7 unless the card gets a real measure; UX says a composer and honest disabled states buy 8.2, and passing 9 needs a day lens the board does not have. The single most-found defect across five seats was that the loudest object on the sheet — the filled-ink Add task pill — did nothing at all, along with all sixteen other chrome controls.

worst.problem: All seventeen chrome controls were dead — not a state change, not a cursor hint, not a live-region word. The most prominent object on the sheet is the one filled-ink pill labelled Add task, and it did nothing; on the empty board the copy reads "Add the first thing you have to do" and there was no working way to do it, so first contact for a venue owner ended in a dead click. Four view tabs and three tools were painted at full strength promising a Schedule and a Calendar nobody has built.
worst.done: Creating a task is real. The composer is a card, not a dialog: it appears in the column it will live in, the caret is already in it, Enter adds, Escape discards, and creation is reversible through the same strip as a completion. The views and tools that do not exist are drawn as unavailable — quiet but legible, since this file's own rule makes ink-4 decorative and never type — and they say why when asked.

worst.problem: Pinning the foot strip to the dock's width left the card's name 81px after three keyboard hints, so the product's signature gesture read "Moving Confi…" at every width measured. Four seats found it independently. A venue owner who cannot tell what she is holding will not use the keyboard model a second time.
worst.done: The strip sizes to its content with the dock's width as a floor, so the foot still reads as one family and can never be narrower than the object it sits on. The hints are one word each. Asserted unclipped at 1440, 1280, 1024, 900 and 768.

worst.problem: The stated ceiling for this seat: the card gave the title 181px at 1440 — twenty-two characters — and nothing is excellent at twenty-two characters. Five columns stretching to fill any sheet also meant the 234px card the specimen sheet declares was only true at one viewport. Separately the rag was unmanaged: "Deposit invoice settled, Mara / & Finn" set 179px against 38px, and the couple's name broke across two lines.
worst.done: The column is bounded at 312 and centred, with `safe` centring because a centred grid that overflows puts its leading content out of reach of its own scroller — which is what the board becomes below 1100. Titles set with text-wrap: balance, re-breaking fifteen of the thirty-two dense titles. Partner names are bound at render, not in the data, because CLIENTS is compared literally and a non-breaking space there would silently drop every card out of client-tag styling.

worst.problem: The board treated an action as a moment rather than as an entry in a history, so both the way back and the operator's place evaporated the instant a second action happened. Operators act in runs; the safety model was built for one action at a time.
worst.done: Every reversible act pushes onto a stack, the strip shows how deep it goes, and Ctrl+Z keeps working after the strip has retired — the strip is news and lives six seconds, the record is history and does not. Reversing an act no longer counts as an act, which is what had made the second undo reach the wrong thing.

worst.problem: Ticking a card destroyed its note. Done is exactly where a venue's memory lives, and "Three asked for dates. Tea urn was the hero. Repeat the format in spring." was invisible on the board it was written on, by any route — the note was gated on the task not being done, and a done card opened nothing.
worst.done: A completed card keeps its note under the same two-line clamp, and click and Enter expand it in place exactly as they do elsewhere.

worst.problem: The chip family carried two units: every chip stated a point in time and the overdue one stated a magnitude, so the reader had to switch. The count of tasks with no day existed only as a bare numeral on a ghost button, its meaning hidden in a title attribute nobody hovers. The overdue chip read as a badge rather than as the control it is.
worst.done: One unit family — every chip is a point in time, with the day count moved to the accessible name and the tooltip. The count with no day is words in the header and opens Planning. The chip is named for what it does, in both states, from the same count that prints its label.

rounds.headline: A full point in one round, and the first seat above 9. Every seat converged on the same theme by a different route: eleven chrome controls were drawn at the weight of a control that works and did nothing at all, including the two whose surface — the Planning drawer — was already fully built and reachable only by editing the URL. Every seat also stated, unprompted, that the remaining distance is a build of hours rather than a redesign or a different decision. Interaction called the behaviour layer itself 9.4 work held down by unmarked dead chrome.

worst.problem: A venue owner meeting this board touches the dock's search field, presses Ctrl K, clicks "Planning 5" and clicks "5 with no date" — the four most inviting targets on the sheet — and gets silence from all four, with nothing at rest telling them why. Six controls already told the truth with aria-disabled and a stated reason; eleven did not. Two of them needed no build at all: the Planning drawer was fully written and rendered under a URL parameter, and onClick simply had no case for it.
worst.done: One helper, applied to every inert control, and they stay in the tab order deliberately — a control that cannot be reached never gets to say why it is missing. Both Planning entry points now open the drawer, which closes the board's largest information gap: nineteen of thirty-two peak-season tasks carry no date and there was no route in the product to give them one. The rail says "outside this design exploration" rather than "not built yet", because Notes and Timeline exist; they are simply not in this artefact.

worst.problem: The Done column inverted the card's own hierarchy. The title dropped to weight 400 while the couple's name stayed at 600, so on a finished card the loudest word was the client and the title was indistinguishable from its own note — on roughly forty per cent of the cards on any populated board. It was the one place in the artefact where the type system actively told a venue owner the wrong thing about what matters.
worst.done: Ink alone carries done — the transparent card, the hairline ring and the filled tick already state it three times over — and the partner name de-escalates with the card instead of outranking it. The whole card steps back together and its internal rank survives.

worst.problem: The composer was the only path in the artefact that destroyed the operator's own typed words, and it did so silently on any repaint: clicking the overdue chip with a half-written task open took the sentence with it. Two of its three exits also dropped focus on <body>, which the source promises twice may never happen.
worst.done: The title is held in state, an open composer keeps focus and the caret across any repaint — being mid-sentence is the worse place to lose — and every exit returns to the control it was opened from. A task created while a filter was on used to be confirmed by name and be nowhere on screen; the filter now releases and says so.

worst.problem: The ghost flew for four hundred milliseconds while the board it left snapped shut in one frame, so the product's one designed moment read as two unrelated events. On a phone the ghost flew to a column that is off screen and left the sheet entirely. Undoing a move played the completion beat on a card that had not been completed.
worst.done: Both trays close and open on the same curve and the same duration as the flight, keyed by id across the repaint. The ghost lands at the board's own edge rather than past it. The check only draws on a card that is actually finished.

worst.problem: The filtered board left four columns describing what they normally hold while holding nothing, and a tray count that openly contradicted the header. Six tooltips said "is not built yet" in a voice this product does not use.
worst.done: Each column says what it is showing under the filter, and the count reads filtered of total. The tooltips say "Board is the only view for now" and "Filter, Sort and Display arrive with the other views".

worst.problem: The composer — the newest headline feature — shipped a micro-label that wrapped every single time, at every width, orphaning one word onto its own line; it was the only two-line mono micro-label in the product. The spine spaced one column of identical tiles two different ways, the product stack on a 4px rhythm and the utility pair below it touching.
worst.done: The hint takes the card foot's own rank and band, in sentence case, so the draft and the card it becomes have the same shape — and on a touch screen it becomes the two controls it was describing. The utility pair joins the spine's rhythm.

rounds.headline: The minimum rose from 8.3 to 8.6 and the spread closed to 0.3 — the tightest the panel has ever been. Five of seven seats named the same thing without conferring: the Planning drawer, promoted into the header in round 8, was shipped as a picture of a room. Fourteen inert controls, a close button that did nothing, no Escape, no focus, and a list read from the fixture rather than the live set. Every seat again volunteered that what remains is hours of building, not a redesign.

worst.problem: The one surface promoted last round was the only one still a rendering. All thirteen of its controls were inert with no aria-disabled and no reason given; it ignored Escape, ignored an outside click, never took focus, and sat twenty-two tab stops from the control that opened it. A stranger who clicks the second lit control in the header hits the dead surface before they ever meet the roving tab stop, the undo strip or the flight.
worst.done: It is a room. It declares itself a dialog with a name, takes focus when it opens, and gives it back to whatever opened it. Escape closes it, the X closes it, clicking away closes it. Its tabs switch the list and carry a roving tab stop, its checkboxes pick, Select all picks and flips to Clear all, and Add a task with no date opens the same composer every other Add opens. Its list is derived from the live set, so the header's count and the drawer's count cannot disagree. Picking a day is the one thing still to build, and it says so.

worst.problem: Nineteen cards print a couple's name and it was dead text — the board's only real grouping, doing nothing. The board could not answer the question a venue opens it to ask: where is Nora and Cian up to.
worst.done: The name is a filter on the identical machinery the overdue chip already proves: one click shows only that couple's work, the strip says whose and offers the way back, Escape clears it. This is the change that turns a workflow view into a venue view, and it cost no colour, no weight and no layout.

worst.problem: The sheet was admitting on screen that it is a lab file. Six tooltips told a venue manager that Notes and Timeline are "outside this design exploration" and five more that a feature is "not built yet" — build status and lab language, in a product that otherwise never breaks character. None of it was reachable on a phone at all.
worst.done: One grammar, present tense, each line naming what does work, and the same sentence is spoken and shown on tap because hover is not available to a thumb.

worst.problem: A scrolled column rendered a bold title at about 40% ink. The mask ramp is 26px and a title's line box is 19px, and with no vertical snap the column rests at any offset, so 92% of resting positions put ink inside the ramp. It was the one place on the sheet that looked like a rendering fault rather than a decision, in the exact state the product exists for.
worst.done: The top edge can be snapped into the gutter; the bottom edge falls wherever the column's height puts it, so no ramp length is safe there. The vertical fades are hairlines now — they say the same thing and never touch a glyph — and the column snaps, so it rests on a card rather than halfway through one.

worst.problem: text-wrap: balance optimises around a float, so on any card carrying a date chip it produced the one-word opening line it exists to prevent — measured rag deltas of 73px, 69px and 53px on a 180px measure.
worst.done: Balance runs only where it earns its place: on titles with no chip beside them. Measured to 11px, 56px and 1px.

worst.problem: Un-completing a task left its completion record on the undo stack, so the board went on offering to redo something already undone. The drawer's count came from the fixture while the header's came from the live set, so the two could contradict each other on screen.
worst.done: Stale records are dropped when the act that made them is reversed, and the drawer derives its list and both tab counts from the same set the header counts.

rounds.headline: The minimum eased from 8.6 to 8.5 as fresh seats found two things nine rounds had missed: the board's loudest claim — one tab stop — was false at fifteen stops, and the card had a ceiling with no floor, so at 1280 it measured 202px against its own documented 258. That second one had survived because every frame in shots/ is captured at 1440, the single width where it is invisible. Brand reached 8.9 and stated plainly that what keeps it off the gate is a dozen strings that were templated rather than written.

worst.problem: The artifact's single loudest claim was false. "One tab stop for the whole board" measured fifteen stops at rest and twenty-seven at peak season, because the couple's name and every column's Add row were tab stops on every card. The assertion that existed to protect the claim counted elements carrying tabindex="0" rather than what a keyboard actually walks, so it was blind to the exact elements breaking it.
worst.done: Both join the roving stop. The gate now counts what is walked, not what carries an attribute, and asserts the number does not grow with the work on the board — five stops at rest, five at peak season. Eleven unavailable controls also guarded the way in; the rail, the switcher and the tools are each one stop the arrows walk, and every stated reason stays reachable.

worst.problem: The card had a ceiling and no floor. At 1280 — a MacBook, all day — it measured 202px against the 258px its own specimen sheet documents: eighteen of thirty-two titles ran to three lines, "High" clipped mid-word, and the Waiting column's wrapped note dropped its first card 17px below the other four so the board lost its shared top baseline. Ten rounds of review never saw it because every frame in shots/ is captured at 1440, the one width where it is invisible.
worst.done: The column has a floor as well as a ceiling. Below about 1400 the board becomes the horizontal scroller it already is at 1200 — the snap, the safe centring and both edge signals were already built and already gate-proven — so there is no discontinuity at the breakpoint. Asserted at four widths.

worst.problem: The header answered four questions the operator did not ask and none of the one they did. On a thirty-two task board the single Due Today chip was the quietest object in the view while one overdue olive order was the loudest, and the two views that would answer the day are drawn but not live.
worst.done: "3 today" sits beside "1 overdue" in the outlined chip grammar the card already uses for the same fact, and it filters the board the same way. The two filters also compose now rather than cancelling each other silently, and Escape unwinds one layer at a time through a single ordered stack.

worst.problem: The rail's six doors were named by a template, so each said the same sentence with a different noun, and the wider "not yet" system carried three verbs, two vocabularies and inconsistent punctuation. The couple-filter sentence had lost its noun and read "Showing the 7 for Mara & Finn" in the most prominent pill on the sheet.
worst.done: Each door names what is behind it. The whole system is one verb, one shape and a terminal stop, and the filter sentence is composed from whichever filters are live rather than branched per filter.

worst.problem: Filtering emptied the column note, which lifted every column body by 16.8px — so the board jumped on the most-clicked control on the page. The hairline that says "there is more below" was painted on the scroller, so a card sitting at the foot was drawn over the very line describing it.
worst.done: The note holds its one-line box when it is empty. The rules are drawn on the tray, above the cards, with the tray told after layout where its own scroller starts and ends.

worst.problem: A card's own words could not be selected — the shell suppresses selection so a drag never starts on a text run, and the exception was never made for the card the operator has opened to read. An open card also read as a hover, because its rule was declared above the interaction block and lost to it. A forced palette threw away every box-shadow, which on this board is the focus ring, the picked-up card, the card's edge and the entire severity language.
worst.done: An open card is the read surface, is not draggable, and its words can be taken. It carries a rank above hover. Every shadow-borne signal is restated in system colours under a forced palette, and the gate drives the board with forced colors active.

rounds.headline: The final round, graded as a finished artifact rather than as work in progress. Seven seats, seven independent verdicts, and they agree: the direction, the palette, the type ramp and the architecture are settled and nothing here asks to reopen them. What separates this from the gate is between two and three focused days of polish and four small builds. Interaction, the harshest seat at 8.2, put the keyboard model "genuinely at or above Linear" and named its remaining distance as "the last week's work that a studio does before it ships". Four regressions this session had introduced were caught and fixed before the record closed.

worst.problem: A forced palette overrode the colour an unfinished tick uses to hide its check, so a high-contrast operator saw a board where all thirteen cards read as done. Introduced by the forced-colors block added in round 10. The drop line and both overflow rules resolved to the page background in the same mode.
worst.done: The check is removed rather than hidden for an unfinished task, and the drop line and the rules are restated in system colours. Asserted with the browser driven in forced-colors mode.

worst.problem: The three card presets set box-shadow directly, at a specificity above the custom property the entire state system is carried in — so in two of the four variants the focus ring, the selection ring and the in-hand lift were simply deleted. The state system and the resting appearance were sharing one property.
worst.done: Rest and state are now two properties: --card-rest is what the card looks like when nothing is happening to it and is what a preset may change; --card-ring is what is happening to it and only the interaction rules may set it. Asserted across all four presets.

worst.problem: releaseUndo() called arm(), and arm() pushes — so every pointer pass over the foot strip added a phantom entry to the undo history and the depth the strip printed was a lie.
worst.done: Releasing the clock re-times the strip; it does not re-record the act. Asserted by passing the pointer over the strip three times and requiring the depth not to move.

worst.problem: The view switcher was given role="tablist" with the roving group in round 10 and its children were never given role="tab" — the only axe-critical violation on the page.
worst.done: Fixed.

worst.problem: STANDING, NOT FIXED. The filtered board is the one screen still visibly undesigned: the answer to "what is late" is one card in a field of four full-height empty columns, with the sentence explaining it 700px below at the foot. Roughly half a day.
worst.done: Left standing. Recorded as the largest single item in the honest distance.

worst.problem: STANDING, NOT FIXED. Emptiness has no design. The zero board and the filtered board are white voids with four identical Add rows and no focal point, and those are the states an operator lives in most.
worst.done: Left standing. Recorded with the filtered state as the same piece of work.
